extracted.intended_audience: general readers, journalists, researchers and practitioners interested in social media moderation and crowd-sourced fact-checking
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic overview of X/Twitter's Community Notes (formerly Birdwatch) describing how notes are proposed, rated, and published, the algorithmic/publication rules, contributor eligibility and incentives, and empirical evaluations of effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bridging-based publication algorithm (diverse-agreement requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Community Notes algorithm publishes notes based on agreement from contributors who have a history of disagreeing; rather than based on majority rule, the program's algorithm prioritizes notes that receive ratings from a 'diverse range of perspectives'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publication requires ratings from both sides of the political spectrum (a 'bridging' requirement). The algorithm's intent is to prioritize notes that bridge differing perspectives rather than simply reflect majority opinion; this mechanism can decrease interaction with the content but also means notes only publish when cross-perspective agreement exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attach verifiable source to notes
rubrics_metrics.description: A source is attached to the note so the information can be verified, in a similar manner to Wikipedia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes should include supporting sources for claims so readers can verify the information. Empirical studies cited on the page evaluated source quality (e.g., a 2024 study found 49% of cited sources were of high quality for a COVID-19 vaccine sample).

rubrics_metrics.name: Contributor ratings: 'Helpful' / 'Not Helpful' and Rating Impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Other contributors give their opinion on the usefulness of the note, identifying notes as 'Helpful' or 'Not Helpful'. Contributors gain points (known as 'Rating Impact') if their ratings are validated, reflecting how helpful a contributor's ratings have been.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ratings by contributors affect whether notes are considered useful and contribute to a contributor's Rating Impact score. Rating Impact is used as an eligibility/weighting factor (see 'opinion classification' and weighting). The system distinguishes between ordinary X users (who can vote on helpfulness) and approved contributors (who can write and provide ratings that factor into publication).

rubrics_metrics.name: Opinion-classification and weighted ratings
rubrics_metrics.description: The program assigns different values to contributors' ratings, categorising users with similar rating histories as a form of 'opinion classification' determined by a vague alignment with the left- and right-wing political spectrum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ratings are weighted rather than counted equally; the bridging algorithm requires that ratings reflect agreement across those classified opinion groups. This weighting and classification affect which notes reach publication and are a central design choice intended to reduce partisan dominance, but the page notes the classification/weighting is vague in description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contributor eligibility, roles, aliases and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Only contributors (who must apply) can write notes; writing is restricted by 'Rating Impact' as well as Community Notes guidelines. Twitter limited visibility of contributors' identities by creating aliases for their accounts to limit bias towards the author of notes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Becoming a contributor requires an application; contributor privileges (ability to write notes) are gated by a contributor's Rating Impact and compliance with guidelines. Aliases are used to obscure contributors' real identities to limit author bias. The page also documents role distinctions such as 'Top Writers' who may have additional privileges (e.g., access to video notes) and pilots where requests are directed to Top Writers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of content eligible for notes
rubrics_metrics.description: Community Notes are often attached to shared articles missing context, misleading advertisements or political tweets with false arguments; they can also note when an image is digitally altered or AI-generated, and have been extended to images, videos and adverts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes have appeared on posts by government accounts, politicians, advertisers' adverts and high-profile public figures. The feature is applied to tweets, images, videos (initially limited to power-users/Top Writers), and adverts; the page gives many examples (White House, FBI, advertisers like Apple/Samsung, and various politicians).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanics for proposing and surfacing notes
rubrics_metrics.description: For a note to be published, a contributor must first propose a note under a tweet; notes in need of ratings by contributors are located under a 'Needs your help' section of the interface.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contributors monitor tweets and replies and propose notes under tweets. Other contributors review notes via the 'Needs your help' queue and mark them Helpful/Not Helpful. In pilots, eligible users can request Community Notes (a threshold of five requests within 24 hours may determine a note being published and direct requests to Top Writers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Incentives and validation points for contributors
rubrics_metrics.description: Contributors get points if their note is validated, known as 'Rating Impact', that reflects how helpful a contributors' ratings have been.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rating Impact functions as both an incentive and a gating metric: contributors accumulate points when their ratings align with published/validated notes, which in turn affects their future influence and ability to write notes. The page links to 'Rating and Writing Impact' documentation for specifics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Framing: notes provide context ('readers added context') rather than explicit 'fact-check' labels
rubrics_metrics.description: The feature does not directly mention fact-checking but instead indicates that 'readers added context'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes are presented as crowd-added contextual information rather than platform-authored fact-check labels; this framing affects user perception and how notes are displayed/worded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational performance metrics: coverage, timeliness and consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Effectiveness is evaluated by whether misleading posts receive notes, how long notes take to appear, and how widely notes are seen; studies found inconsistent application and delays in publishing notes for major events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple studies cited: examples include average times to appear (one study average 7 hours, over 50% within 8 hours but many taking longer), high percentages of top misinformation failing to receive notes (e.g., NewsGuard and other reports citing 68% or 74% failing to receive notes in sampled datasets), and notes often being seen by a small fraction of total viewers of the original posts. These operational factors are treated as implicit criteria for Community Notes' quality and impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency/open-source availability of code and data
rubrics_metrics.description: Community Notes adopted an open-source approach; the system's code and data are public, and proponents argue this transparency should make manipulation obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open-source publication of code/data is cited as a defense against covert manipulation: proponents (including platform leadership) claim openness enables detection of gaming or manipulation. The page records claims and counterclaims about whether openness suffices to detect or prevent manipulation.
